Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 24 November 1943, at half past two in the afternoon, open with a warm exchange over Thanksgiving. Sir Alan Brooke had arranged for a service in Cairo cathedral the next evening, and Admiral Leahy accepted the British invitation with thanks on behalf of the American chiefs.

The main business is machinery for cooperation with the Soviet Union and China, under papers C.C.S. 406 and 406/1. Brooke argues that a standing United Chiefs of Staff with real power would sit awkwardly above the combined body, since Russia and China fight different enemies. The chiefs agree to propose nothing themselves, to resist a standing committee if pressed, and for now to invite Soviet and Chinese officers to conference sessions touching their own concerns.

Charles Bohlen's minutes record a meeting between President Roosevelt and Marshal Stalin at Tehran on 29 November 1943, at a quarter to three in the afternoon. Much of it is Roosevelt handing over papers and opening the question of the postwar peace organization.

Roosevelt lends Stalin a report by an American officer who spent six months with Tito in Yugoslavia. He also gives him papers on shuttle-bombing bases in Russia. More papers cover air and naval planning against Japan. Throughout, he stresses the strictest secrecy. He then sketches his world organization: a large United Nations body making recommendations, and a smaller executive committee of the Big Four plus six other states, handling non-military questions. Stalin probes whether that committee could bind nations, noting it could in fact force compliance, and Roosevelt agrees.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d465:

Hopkins had been at Roosevelt's side through the first meeting with Stalin. The State Department later printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

A direct Hopkins-to-Molotov line was one of the warmest channels between Washington and Moscow, built on Hopkins's earlier missions to the Soviet Union. Coming straight after Tehran, the message belongs to the work of holding the new three-way partnership together. arxiv-2606-04865: Coulomb-mediated interactions of charge-transfer excitons were studied in TMD lateral heterostructures. The 2D materials physics was measured. The finding serves condensed matter physics. Coulomb forces mediate exciton interactions. Sonowal measured exciton Coulomb interactions. Optoelectronics needs exciton physics. Sonowal's excitons enable 2D lasers.
arxiv-2606-05565: The Lévy dragon is a fractal — an infinitely detailed shape born from simple rules. This paper studies its revolving structure and how linear transforms reshape it, charting the symmetries hidden in its coils. The work extends our understanding of how fractals tile and transform the plane.
arxiv-2606-06065: Training one speech model for two related outputs — multi-task learning — sounds efficient, but the representations can tangle. This paper shows multi-task learning is not enough for dual-output second language speech recognition: representational entanglement degrades both tasks. Diagnosing the tangle is the first step to undoing it.
arxiv-2606-06165: Nonlinear and stochastic multiscale PDEs — the equations of real materials and climates — defeat classical computers. This paper attacks them with Young-measure-based quantum linear programming algorithms: quantum methods that handle the equations' wild oscillations. The work maps a path from quantum hardware to practical simulation.
arxiv-2606-06265: Ensembles combine many predictors, but not all members deserve equal say. This paper builds a robust ensemble of selectively strengthened and augmented predictors — boosting the reliable ones, augmenting the training of the shaky ones. Selective strengthening makes the crowd wiser than any individual.
arxiv-2606-06665: Emotions spread through social networks — but do AI agent networks catch feelings the same way humans do? This paper compares sentiment contagion in AI-agent and human social networks, with evidence from MOLTBOOK. The comparison reveals whether artificial societies feel like real ones.
arxiv-2606-00065: Extracting materials data from scientific literature needs more than text and tables — it needs vision. This paper integrates vision-language models into ComProScanner for that extraction. The integration reads figures like a materials scientist. Scientific figures hold valuable extractable data. Modern vision models can extract it reliably.
tob-10465:
John Calvin's Institutes of the Christian Religion stands as the landmark system of Protestant theology, and volume one lays its foundations. Calvin, a French reformer trained in law, wrote with lawyerly precision and a preacher's fire. Readers begin where he begins: with knowledge of God and knowledge of ourselves.

Early books ask what humans can know of God, why Scripture is trustworthy, and how God governs creation and human life. Calvin argues each point in ordered chapters meant to teach pastors and students. Together with its companion volume, the work gave the Reformation its most complete statement of faith and shaped Reformed churches for centuries.
tob-10565:
Hafiz of Shiraz, who lived in fourteenth-century Persia, wrote lyric poems called ghazals that Persians still quote by heart. Gertrude Lowthian Bell, a traveler and scholar of the Middle East, chose poems from his Divan and turned them into English verse. Her versions introduced many English readers to Hafiz.

Again and again the poems sing of nightingales and roses, cups of wine, and a Beloved who is hard to reach. Sufi readers hear divine love behind those images, while others hear earthly romance. Bell keeps the playfulness and longing that made Hafiz the most loved poet of his land.
tob-4165:
George William Cox built The Mythology of the Aryan Nations on the solar theory: nearly every hero tale, he held, retells the drama of dawn, sun, and storm in disguise. Volume two applies that key across the Indo-European world, from India to Greece to the Norse north. The book appeared in 1870.

Cox writes with sweep and total confidence, unlocking myth after myth with the same bright key. Later scholarship broke with the solar school entirely, and Lang mocked it without mercy. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. The volume survives as a grand fossil of Victorian method.
tob-4265:
John Ferguson, a Glasgow professor of chemistry, catalogued the James Young collection of alchemical books in his Bibliotheca Chemica. Volume two continues the great bibliography: author by author, edition by edition, the literature of alchemy is listed with a scholar's patience. The catalogue appeared from the collection formed in 1908's record.

Ferguson notes printers, dates, contents, and the worth of each item, turning a private library into the map of a whole field. Alchemy's historians still begin their hunts in his pages. Verified from the 1919 edition, volume two completes the standard guide to who wrote what in the hermetic centuries.
shoo-king-legge-1865:
James Legge translated the Shoo King as volume three of The Chinese Classics in 1865. The Shoo King, or Book of Documents, holds China's oldest state papers. Legge was a Scottish missionary and a great scholar of Chinese.

Speeches, decrees, and counsels from early kings fill the text. Rulers speak of the mandate of heaven and just rule. Legge adds long notes to guide Western readers through the lore. The book is a Confucian treasure and a record of statecraft. It remains a base source for early Chinese history in English.
lubbock-prehistoric-times-1865:
John Lubbock, a banker and neighbor of Darwin, published Pre-historic Times in 1865 and founded a discipline in the act. Lubbock coined the words Palaeolithic and Neolithic, the Old and New Stone Ages, which archaeology still uses. His book systematized the Stone Age from ancient remains.

He sorts stone tools, lake dwellings, and burial mounds into their ages, then turns to living peoples for light on ancient customs. The manners of modern peoples he called savages are read as survivals of the earliest human life. The method is dated and its language of its time. The framework lasted: this was the most cited prehistory of its generation.
baring-gould-book-of-were-wolves-1865:
Sabine Baring-Gould hoards all lore of the wolf man in The Book of Were-Wolves, his study of 1865. Baring-Gould was a priest, squire, and scribe of vast range. He draws on tales, trials, and myths from Greece to the north lands. Wolf men prowl in most: men who turn beast, feast on flesh, and are slain at last by cross, steel, or fire.

He asks what truth lies back of the tales: mad men, wild faiths, or worse. His tone is grave, rich, and full of strange scraps. The book founds the study of the theme in English.
beast-of-gevaudan-annual-register-1765:
News from France tells of a beast that kills in the Annual Register piece of 1765. In the hills of Gevaudan, a great wolf like beast had slain maids and herds in scores. Hunts by troops, lords, and the king's own gun men failed to stop it. The English piece sums the dread as word of it crossed the sea in that grim year.

No firm name or kind is set in the text. It is a raw note from the midst of the scare. Fans of wolf lore cite it as a first source. Its brevity is its punch.
maxwell-dynamical-theory-electromagnetic:
James Clerk Maxwell, a Scots sage of the first rank, read this memoir on the field of electric force in 1865. He built it from the work of Faraday and from his own maths. Its aim was to join three fields that men had kept apart.

Maxwell's sums show that electric force, magnetism, and light are one thing in three forms. Light, in his scheme, is a wave in the same field that moves the compass needle. The claim set the tests that Michelson would try in the years to come, with strange results.
blumenbach-anthropological-treatises-186:
Johann Friedrich Blumenbach was a German sage who shaped the study of man in the late 1700s. Thomas Bendyshe turned his Latin works into English in this set of 1865. Blumenbach worked from skulls, which he hoarded from all parts of the world.

His most famed scheme sorts mankind into five races by skull shape and skin tone. That scheme set the frame for the study of the body of man through the next hundred years. The set lets the reader see the scheme and its proof in the maker's own words.
fuhlrott-neanderthal-1865:
Johann Carl Fuhlrott, a school master in Elberfeld, was the man who first saw the worth of the Neanderthal bones. Quarry men found them in a cave in the Neander valley in 1856. This book of 1865 is his full case in German for their great age.

Fuhlrott holds that the bones are fossil, the relics of a race from deep in the past. He sets out the cave, the bones, and the scorn his claim drew from the learned world. The book is the find claim writ large, by the man who stood by it first.
barnum-humbugs-world-1865:
P. T. Barnum, the great American showman, wrote this book on the frauds of the world in 1865. He knew the theme at first hand, for he had run some famed frauds of his own. His aim was to show how the public loves to be fooled, and pays for it.

He tells the tale of his Feejee Mermaid, a stitched fake shown as a true maid of the sea. Ghosts, quack cures, and stock frauds of his age fill the rest of the brisk book. The showman's own word on his tricks makes the book a rare, frank source.
spallanzani-saggio-microscopiche-1765:
Lazzaro Spallanzani was an Italian priest and keen worker with the microscope. His Saggio of 1765, in Italian, took on John Needham and Buffon. Those men held that life can spring from dead broth on its own. Spallanzani set out to test the claim with care.

He boiled broths in sealed flasks and showed that no small life forms grew. Air shut out, the broth stayed clear and pure for weeks. His tests made the rule that life comes from life the norm. The book, part of his 1765 pair of tracts, is a root text of the field.
thoreau-cape-cod-1865:
Henry David Thoreau's Cape Cod saw print in 1865, after his death, his book of the sea-shore. The posthumous travel narrative gathers four trips to the Cape between 1849 and 1857 in one volume. Many rank it the great American book of the sea-shore, salt, wreck, and dune in prose.

Thoreau walks the Great Beach from Eastham to Provincetown, past wrecks, lighthouses, and wreckers' huts on the sand. The wreck of the St. John, with drowned Irish emigrants, opens the book in scenes of stark pity. Wellfleet oystermen, surfmen, and keepers give him Cape lore, humor, and a pagan love of the sea. His eye turns a bare sand arm into a world of history, weather, and wild life. The book is his sunniest and saltiest, a shore walk that never dates.
ruskin-sesame-lilies-1865:
John Ruskin published Sesame and Lilies in 1865, two lectures that became his most popular book. The first lecture, on reading, urges care in choosing and studying great books. Kings' treasuries is his image for the wealth stored in literature. The second lecture treats women's education and duties, in terms of his age.

Ruskin argues that girls deserve serious schooling, though within a separate sphere. Modern readers debate that second lecture sharply. The first lecture remains a classic plea for deep reading. Ruskin's prose here is at its most musical and direct. The book shows the Victorian essay and lecture at their height.
arnold-essays-criticism-1865:
Matthew Arnold published Essays in Criticism, First Series, in 1865, a landmark in literary study. The opening essay, The Function of Criticism at the Present Time, argues for disinterested inquiry. Criticism, Arnold says, must see the object as it really is and spread the best ideas. Other essays treat poets and prose writers of Europe.

He writes on Homer, Heine, and the Celtic element in literature, among other topics. His touchstone idea judges verse by great lines held in mind. The book in effect invented modern literary criticism as a public task in English. Arnold's calm, lucid style set its tone. Scholars still teach these essays.
comte-positivism-bridges-1865:
Auguste Comte published A General View of Positivism in French in 1848. The English text here is J. H. Bridges's translation of 1865. Comte sums up his system for general readers. Positivism, he argues, can reorganize society after revolution's chaos. Science gives the method, and the religion of humanity gives the bond.

He outlines a positivist polity with priests of humanity, festivals, and a new calendar of secular saints. Many readers admired the science and balked at the religion. Bridges led the English positivist movement that spread Comte's ideas. The book is Comte's own shortest summary of his thought. It shows both his power and his strangeness.
lecky-rationalism-1865:
W. E. H. Lecky published his history of rationalism in Europe in 1865. The full title traces the rise and influence of the spirit of rationalism. Lecky studies the decline of belief in magic, witchcraft, and miracles. He also treats persecution, skepticism, and the growth of science and industry.

His thesis is Whig history at its best: reason slowly defeats fear and dogma. Lecky marshals cases from trials, laws, and sermons across centuries. The book made his reputation while he was still young. Modern scholars nuance his story, yet its sweep impresses. It is a great Victorian argument for the power of free inquiry.
suso-life-knox-1865:
Henry Suso was a German Dominican friar of the fourteenth century, famed for harsh penance and tender visions of Christ. His Life, written by himself with the help of a devoted nun, appears here in Knox's 1865 translation. The book is a medieval spiritual classic in its own right.

Suso tells of wearing a hair shirt and an iron-studded cross, then of learning to leave such rigors for inner stillness. He records dreams, temptations, and talks with his spiritual daughter in plain, moving detail. English readers met here a mystic both severe and gentle, shaped by suffering into patience.
lightfoot-galatians-1865:
Lightfoot's commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Galatians, in this 1896 edition, is the work that revolutionized English New Testament scholarship. Lightfoot treats the short letter as a doorway into Paul's whole world. Galatians, where Paul defends his gospel against rival teachers, rewards his close method.

He prints the Greek text with essays on the letter's date, its readers, and the history of the early church in Galatia. His notes weigh grammar, custom, and geography before drawing any doctrine from a verse. Students of Paul still learn the craft of commentary from Lightfoot's example. The commentary teaches by example how much a short letter can hold.
hooke-micrographia-1665:
Robert Hooke published Micrographia in 1665 in London, the first major work of microscopy. Hooke, curator of experiments for the Royal Society, drew what the microscope showed him and printed the drawings as large fold-out plates. Readers saw a flea, a louse, and the edge of a razor as never before.

In the pores of cork Hooke saw tiny boxes, and he named them cells, a word biology still uses. He also studied crystals, plants, and insects, and guessed at the wave nature of light. The Royal Society backed the book, and Samuel Pepys sat up all night with it. Micrographia taught Europe to look closely.
galileo-two-new-sciences-salusbury-1665:
Galileo's Two New Sciences, written in 1638, appears here in Thomas Salusbury's 1665 English translation, Mathematical Discourses Concerning Two New Sciences. Salusbury had planned a full English Galileo; this part survived fire and neglect to reach print. It was the first English form of Galileo's last book.

The discourses treat the strength of beams and materials and the laws of falling bodies and projectiles. Galileo's speakers test claims with thought experiments, such as dropping weights tied together. Salusbury's version, though rough in places, put the founding text of modern mechanics into English within a generation. The Crew translation of 1914 later replaced it for most readers.
swinburne-atalanta-calydon-1865:
Algernon Charles Swinburne was an Oxford undergraduate with a passion for Greek tragedy when he wrote Atalanta in Calydon. Published in 1865, the verse drama made him famous at twenty-eight. Swinburne shaped it closely on the plays of Aeschylus, with a full Greek chorus.

The story retells the hunt of the Calydonian boar, sent by the goddess Artemis to punish a slighted altar. Atalanta, the swift huntress, draws first blood, and the hero Meleager gives her the prize. Family pride and a mother's curse then doom Meleager himself. The choruses, rich with fate and springtime, are the glory of the work. It led the Greek revival in Victorian poetry.
kardec-le-ciel-et-l-enfer-1865:
Le Ciel et l'Enfer became the fourth book of Kardec's Spiritist canon in 1865. The Paris first edition is the text preserved here, in French. Kardec examines divine justice through the lens of Spiritism. Death, heaven, hell, and purgatory all come under review.

Spirit communications supply much of his evidence about the afterlife. He sorts the states of souls after death by their moral condition. Suffering, in his account, corrects rather than damns forever. An English version from 1878 survives only in libraries, with no free scan. The French original thus serves as the documentary edition. Spiritist readers rank it beside his other canon books.
kircher-mundus-subterraneus-1665:
Athanasius Kircher, the Jesuit whose learning seemed to cover everything, published Mundus Subterraneus in 1665. Twelve books map the world beneath our feet: volcanoes, quakes, caves, and a great central fire. Kircher drew on reports from travelers and his own descent toward a volcano's crater.

The Latin original is staged here as a documentary text, since no public-domain English version exists. Plates show dragons, giants' bones, and the earth's inner channels as Kircher imagined them. Wrong in many claims, the work still stands as the grand baroque picture of geology before the science had a name.
tylor-researches-into-the-early-history-:
Edward Burnett Tylor published this first great work in 1865, six years before Primitive Culture made his name. In it he laid out the methods that would define early anthropology: comparing customs across peoples to trace how civilization grew.

Tylor argued for the psychic unity of mankind, the idea that all peoples share the same basic mind. He studied gesture language, counting, myths, and the survivals, old customs that linger as clues to earlier stages. His evidence ranges from children's games to funeral rites. The book shows a new science being built, one comparison at a time.
livingstone-zambesi-expedition-1865:
David Livingstone led a government expedition up the Zambesi from 1858 to 1864. His Narrative of an Expedition to the Zambesi and Its Tributaries appeared in 1865. His brother Charles and the geologist John Kirk were among the party.

The steam launch Ma Robert proved too weak for the river, and the Kebrabasa rapids blocked the way inland. Still, the party mapped the Shire highlands and reached Lake Nyasa, which Livingstone claimed for science. The Universities' Mission that followed met disaster, costing Bishop Mackenzie his life. Livingstone writes with honesty about failure, fevers, and the slave trade he saw growing.
plos-pone-0003465:
Abdiaziz S. Mohamood and co-authors studied how the immune system prunes T cells in this 2008 paper. A pathway called Fas orders extra or faulty T cells to die. Which T cell groups that pathway controls in the body was poorly defined. Most mature T cells carry either CD4 or CD8 markers.

The team found Fas constantly purging one odd group, double negative T cells. Removing those cells shapes the mix of the wider T cell pool. Steady pruning keeps the immune repertoire in balance. It may also guard against attacks on the body's own tissues.
plos-pone-0003565:
Lia E. Perez and co-authors studied a brake on platelet-making cells in this 2008 paper. A phosphatase called SHIP-1 dials down signals from cytokine receptors. Those signals help drive megakaryocytopoiesis, the making of platelet parent cells. Thrombopoietin is one of the key signals involved.

The authors tested whether SHIP-1 controls early megakaryocyte progenitors. It negatively influenced those early cells in their assays. A brake at that stage sets later platelet output. Disorders of too many or too few platelets may involve this control. Platelet counts must stay in a tight range to keep blood clotting safe.
plos-pone-0003665:
Tjeerd G. Kimman, Sander Banus, Naomi Reijmerink, and colleagues published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Protection after whooping cough vaccination differs from child to child. The team studied genes in the Toll-like receptor pathway, a set of sensors that help start immune responses.

They linked combinations of these genes to the strength of the antibody response after pertussis vaccination. Single genes alone did not tell the story; interacting genes did. The work suggests vaccine response is a property of the immune wiring as a whole, not of one part.
plos-pone-0003765:
Tong Zhou, Peter J. Enyeart, and Claus O. Wilke published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. When selection favors a protein's new function, mutations can pile up in a small stretch of DNA. Such clusters are fingerprints of adaptation. An earlier method for finding them had a flaw involving solvent exposure.

The authors present an improved way to detect clusters of mutations. Their approach accounts for how buried or exposed each site in a protein is. It separates the marks of positive selection from random noise more cleanly than the method it revises.
plos-pone-0003865:
Travis I. Moore, Ching-Shan Chou, Qing Nie, and colleagues published this yeast study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Moving or growing up a chemical gradient is a universal behavior of living things. Baker's yeast cells do it when they follow the mating pheromone alpha-factor toward a partner.

The team tested yeast a-cells in a microfluidics chamber that held a steady pheromone gradient. The cells sensed the gradient across their own tiny surface and responded robustly. The work shows single cells navigating by smell with precision, despite noise in the signal.
plos-pone-0003965:
Stéphane Hausmann, Jean-Baptiste Marq, Caroline Tapparel, and co-authors studied a virus sensor in cells in 2008. Most RNA viruses start copying with building blocks that leave tagged RNA ends. Cells use a sensor called RIG-I to spot such RNA. That spotting switches on interferon-beta, an antiviral alarm.

Their PLOS ONE article examines how double-stranded RNA triggers that alarm. Many viruses depend on RIG-I detection to be noticed at all, they note. Pinning down the trigger sharpens models of early immune defense. It also informs design of vaccines that use RNA signals. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004065:
Jérôme Sueur, Sandrine Pavoine, Olivier Hamerlynck, and co-authors proposed listening as a biodiversity survey tool in 2008. Counting species is among the hardest tasks in conservation work. Habitat loss keeps raising the urgency of fast assessments. Sound offers a shortcut where many animals call.

Their PLOS ONE article tests a rapid acoustic survey for appraisal. Recorded soundscapes can index how rich a site is. The approach covers large areas faster than trapping or transects. It will not name every species, but it ranks sites for protection. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004165:
Hans-Martin Herz and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In yeast, a set of genes builds the ESCRT complexes, sorting machines that route proteins at the early endosome, a cell's sorting station. In the fruit fly, faults in one ESCRT-II part, vps25, cause sorting defects, a build-up of Notch protein, and excess Notch signalling.

The team compared the fly's ESCRT-II components, looking for what they share and where they differ. Their genetic tests separate common duties from unique ones within the complex. The results clarify how this sorting machinery controls signals that guide growth and development.
plos-pone-0004365:
Gabriele Hörmannsperger and colleagues published this probiotic study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The probiotic mixture VSL#3 is a blend of live bacteria used for gut health. Clinical and lab studies suggest it protects patients in inflammatory bowel disease, a long-term inflammation of the gut. How its bacteria calm that inflammation, strain by strain, was not clear.

The team worked with intestinal epithelial cells, the cells lining the gut. They tracked IP-10, a chemokine that calls immune cells to a site. They report that the bacteria block IP-10 release after the protein is made, a post-translational effect. That is one way friendly bacteria can calm an inflamed gut.
plos-pone-0004465: In 2009, Dupierrix, Gresty, and Ohlmann spun volunteers' keen sense of direction. Long-lasting egocentric disorientation followed normal sensori-motor spatial play sessions. The volunteers lost their bearings for many hours. The finding maps the brain's inner compass. The odd effect was deeply surprising.
plos-pone-0004565: In 2009, Goodin proposed a neat three-step cascade for multiple sclerosis. The causal cascade leading to multiple sclerosis was modeled. Genetic risk plus environmental hits stacked up in order. The model frames MS pathogenesis thinking anew. The exact sequence matters hugely.
plos-pone-0004665: In 2009, Basso, Martinez, and Manso tracked a fruit fly pest's deep Argentine roots. Genetic polymorphisms within and between founder populations of Ceratitis capitata were mapped. The medfly's invasion genetics emerged clearly. The finding informs pest control. The pest is major.
plos-pone-0004765: In 2009, Higashi, Ishikawa, and Yu linked a motility protein to a brain-tumor switch. Human Mena associated with Rac1 small GTPase in glioblastoma cell lines. The motility protein partnered the switch well. The study maps cancer invasion. The protein family is Ena/VASP.
stowe-household-papers-1865:
Household Papers and Stories collects Stowe's magazine pieces on home life. The Riverside printing of 1896 places it as volume eight of her writings, with a portrait and a view of her Hartford home. Copyright entries reach back to 1864 and 1868 for parts of the material.

Short and warm pieces treat children, servants, and the small morals of each day. Stowe jokes about fussy housekeepers and writes with care about marriage and kin. Readers who knew only Uncle Tom's Cabin met a new Stowe here. She sounds less like a reformer and more like a wise friend beside the American fireside.
bernard-medecine-experimentale-1865:
Claude Bernard lays down the rules for studying life in his Introduction to experimental medicine, in French from 1865. Living bodies, he insists, obey fixed laws like any matter. The doctor must test ideas by trial, control, and close watch, never by dogma or mere authority alone.

His notion of the body's inner balance, its internal environment, proved fertile for all later physiology. Bernard writes as a working scientist teaching a method, step by step. Few medical books have shaped their field so deeply. The volume stands as the charter of modern physiology, still read wherever the lab method is taught.
voting-rights-act-1965:
Congress passed the Voting Rights Act in 1965, months after Selma's violence. Bloody Sunday on the Pettus Bridge led straight to this law. At last the ballot gains real federal teeth in the South.

Literacy tests are banned as tools to bar Black voters from polls. Federal registrars go south to enroll voters whom locals turned away. Counties with rigged rolls fall under strict federal watch for years. Black officeholders rise fast once the vote becomes truly open. The most effective civil rights statute ever passed remade American politics for good. Within a few years, Black voter rolls in the South had transformed.
jevons-coal-question-1865:
William Stanley Jevons published The Coal Question in 1865, asking whether Britain's prosperity could outlast its coal. Britain's factories, ships, and railways all ran on coal, and use was climbing steeply each year. Jevons, a young economist and logician, did the sums that few others had bothered to do.

He showed that coal use grew at a steady compound rate, so that even vast reserves would be strained within a few generations. He also noted a trap: more efficient engines did not save coal but spread its use, a pattern still called the Jevons paradox. Gladstone read the book and spoke of the national debt in its light. The work made Jevons famous overnight and stands as the first great study of resource limits, foreseeing the energy debates of a century later.
cia-0000007865:
Two sharp items share a CIA cable dated March 1965: a rebel leader asking for asylum, and a machine-gun killing. The heading names Rafael Boni in connection with the killing, though the surviving title breaks off mid-name. Traffic of this kind moved fast and carried little polish.

Short cables formed the daily feed from which larger judgments were built. An asylum plea could shift local politics, while a single killing could signal wider unrest. Read together, the items show field reporting at its rawest, before analysts sorted rumor from fact. The declassified file preserves that first, rough draft of events.
cia-0000009565:
A North Vietnamese air defense unit killed an American pilot, a September 1972 CIA report states. The heading admits key facts were unknown: when the report was published and when the event occurred. Soviet-built missiles and guns had made the north's skies deadly for years.

Even with dates missing, the report entered the loss record for matching against missing crews. Air defense kills often left no witnesses on the American side. A claim from the other side's weapons units could be the only evidence. The file shows analysts working with scraps, honestly labeled as scraps, in the air war's final autumn.
cia-0000009865:
North Vietnamese forces captured Lao, South Vietnamese, and American troops near a place the title cuts short, an April 1968 item reports. The capture's mixed roll shows the Laos war's true cast: three nations' soldiers taken in one action. The year 1968 brought the war's widest fighting.

Joint captures complicated every record, since three armies kept three sets of books. A man could be a prisoner in one file and missing in another. Reports naming all three groups helped align those books. This file preserves one alignment point, a single action with prisoners from every side of the secret war.
cia-0000012365:
Material received on August 27 needed forwarding, and a note from July 1962 records the errand with the forwarder's name blacked out. The note belongs to the Penkovsky pipeline, the physical path secrets traveled. Cutouts and couriers carried the colonel's product by hand before analysts ever saw it, and each handoff left a paper trace like this one.

The logistics were the operation's unglamorous spine. Secrets in transit were secrets at risk, and the files logged their movements with care. For readers, the note shows the hands a spy's harvest passed through on its way to power.
cia-0000014765: The pro-Cominform Communist Party protested the Rosenberg case in the Free Territory of Trieste, in a CIA file dated January 5, 1953. Two causes met in one small city: Trieste's own status, and the New York trial. The protest shows how fast the Rosenberg cause crossed oceans. Local parties folded it into their own fights.
cia-0000015265: Flying objects were seen in the Saransk area, in a CIA report dated October 1, 1955. Saransk lay in the middle Volga lands of the Soviet Union. Reports from deep inside the USSR were prized and doubted at once. The file keeps one such claim from a town few Americans could have named.
cia-0000015365: Current status of the Unidentified Flying Objects project fills a CIA file dated November 4, 1953. The project is named UFOB in the title's code. A status note means the work had bosses who wanted progress in writing. By late 1953 the project was sorting sightings in a steady, clerks' rhythm. The UFOB status report is kept in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015465: Spain and North Africa produced flying saucer reports in a CIA record dated July 3, 1952. That summer ranks among the busiest of the whole saucer era in America and Europe. Southern reports widened the map well past the Atlantic world. The agency gathered them country by country, building a world picture of a wave that no single office could explain away.
cia-0000022365: Belgrade's Serbian radio carried the Powers trial, a CIA record dated in 1960 reports. Yugoslavia stood outside both blocs, so its airwaves reached listeners East and West. Carrying the Moscow trial gave Belgrade a neutral stage in a superpower quarrel. The entry shows the trial's audience stretching well past the courtroom and the two rival capitals.
cia-0000036565:
A CIA report dated March 3, 1969 covers Daniel R. Nidds under the Bright Light project. Bright Light was the effort to find and account for Americans missing or held prisoner in Southeast Asia. The report is one case file inside that much larger search.

Inside, the focus stays on one man: what was known about Nidds and what remained unclear. Case files like this were built piece by piece from sightings, lists, and witness accounts. Adams dealt most often with Lord John Russell, Britain's foreign secretary. His letters home summed up those talks and the mood of the British government. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d365:
From the British legation in Washington on 19 January 1863, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 365 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Lyons reported each exchange to Lord John Russell in London. What he wrote to Seward, and what Seward answered, shaped British choices about the war. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d465:
A 16 April 1863 dispatch from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington reached William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. frus-1863p1-d665:
The 16 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0000065:
Yoav Soen, Daniel S. Chen, Daniel L. Kraft, and others reported a new lab method in PLOS Biology in 2003. Their tool uses tiny chip arrays of peptides held by MHC proteins. Those pairs are what T cells scan when they check whether a cell is healthy or infected.

Finding which T cells react to which peptide is slow work with older tools. A chip that tests many pairs at once can spot and sort reactive T cells far faster. That kind of map helps researchers track immune responses during infection or after a vaccine. It can also aid work on immune diseases, where the wrong T cells attack the body's own tissues.
plos-pbio-0020065:
Guang Yao, Mark Craven, Norman Drinkwater, and co-workers used yeast to map a toxic response pathway in PLOS Biology in 2004. The aryl hydrocarbon receptor is a vertebrate protein that reacts to dioxins and similar pollutants. It switches genes on and off, with effects that include harm to development.

Yeast lacks the receptor, which makes it a clean test bed. The team placed the pathway's parts into yeast and charted the contacts between them, step by step. That kind of map is hard to draw in animal cells, where many signals overlap. Their work lists the players in order and gives toxicology a clearer wiring diagram to test with new compounds.
plos-pbio-0020365:
Mikhail A. Lebedev, Adam Messinger, Jerald D. Kralik, and their team recorded from monkey prefrontal cortex in PLOS Biology in 2004. This front brain area handles planning and working memory. Monkeys did a task where the spot they attended and the spot they had to remember were sometimes different.

Nerve cells in the area coded both kinds of spots, letting the authors compare the two codes side by side. Knowing how attention and memory share or split cell resources is a basic question in brain science. The study gives hard data for models of how the front brain juggles what it sees now with what it must hold for later.
plos-pone-0000065:
Thomas Ruf, Teresa Valencak, Frieda Tataruch, and their team compared mammal running speeds in PLOS ONE in 2006. They found faster mammals tend to have more of a certain fat, called n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid, in their muscle membranes. The pattern held across species of very different sizes.

Cell membranes rich in these fats let pumps and signals work faster, which may support quicker muscle action. That would explain why speed tracks membrane makeup so well. The idea links diet and fat chemistry to peak performance in a broad way. It is a neat case of a small chemical trait scaling up to a whole-animal ability that anyone can watch.
plos-pone-0000165:
Juliet R. C. Pulliam, Jonathan G. Dushoff, Simon A. Levin, and colleagues published this modeling paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines epidemic enhancement in populations where people are only partially immune. Enhancement means a disease can spread or sicken more, not less, when some immunity is already present.

Partial immunity is the norm for many real diseases, from dengue to flu. The authors model when it helps transmission instead of hindering it. Their results warn disease modelers that immunity cannot always be treated as a simple shield, a point with direct bearing on vaccine policy.
plos-pone-0000265:
Piers D. L. Howe and Margaret S. Livingstone published this vision paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Hermann grid illusion is a classic: stare at a grid of black squares and grey spots seem to appear at the crossings. The authors use the cancellation technique, adjusting a real stimulus to null out the illusion, to put a number on its strength.

Measuring an illusion precisely lets researchers test competing explanations of it. The cancellation method turns a subjective effect into a quantity. The paper gives vision science a firmer grip on one of its oldest puzzles, which probes how the retina and brain process contrast.
plos-pone-0000365:
Miguel Viveiros and co-authors examined in PLOS ONE in 2007 how the gut bacterium E. coli responds when antibiotics stress it. Their study links three things. It joins the pressure the drug puts on the cell and the genes the cell switches on in reply. It also tracks changes in how easily things pass through the cell's outer wall.

How permeable a bacterium's wall is can decide whether an antibiotic reaches its target inside. By tying gene responses to wall changes, the study addresses a core problem in drug resistance: bacteria that keep drugs out can survive treatment. The work fits the wider effort to understand how common bacteria adapt to the medicines used against them.
plos-pone-0000465:
Simon Melov and colleagues reported that exercise training rewound gene activity patterns of aging muscle, in PLOS ONE in 2007. As people age, skeletal muscle weakens and its gene expression shifts in characteristic ways. The team tested whether resistance exercise, weight training, could reverse that aging pattern in human skeletal muscle.

The title states their conclusion: resistance exercise reverses aging in human skeletal muscle, at least at the level of gene activity. That molecular evidence complements what trainers observe, that older adults regain strength with training. It also gives researchers measurable markers for testing other interventions meant to slow muscle aging.
plos-pone-0000565:
Nurit Kalderon and colleagues combined two strategies to treat spinal cord injury in an animal model, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The injury was an acute spinal cord contusion, a bruise like those from car crashes. Their therapeutic strategy paired cell elimination, removing harmful cells, with microsurgical intervention.

Spinal cord injury damages tissue twice: at impact, and again through inflammation and cell death in the hours after. A combined strategy addresses both waves. Studies like this test combinations because single treatments have repeatedly disappointed in this field, where even modest preserved function changes a patient's life.
plos-pone-0000665:
Kimberly A. Kelly, Jonathan Carson, Jason R. McCarthy and co-authors created a peptide tag for imaging inside living bodies, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Probes that label specific proteins have become critical for watching biological processes. The team used phage display, a screening method with viruses, to find a short peptide that binds near-infrared fluorochromes very tightly.

They call the peptide the IQ-tag. Near-infrared light passes through tissue better than visible light, so labels glowing in that range suit in vivo imaging. The title says the tag allows protein and cell specific labeling. A small, tight-binding tag can be attached to many targets, widening what doctors and researchers can see.
plos-pone-0000765:
Santanu Mukherjee, Mahmoud Abd-El-Latif, Michal Bronstein and colleagues studied how a small virus builds its shell, in PLOS ONE in 2007. SV40 is a small DNA virus without an envelope, wrapped in an icosahedral capsid 45 nanometers wide. The outer shell is composed of pentamers, five-unit clusters, of the major capsid protein VP1, linked by flexible arms at their tails.

Assembly builds the shell from those capsomers around the viral minichromosome. The title highlights high cooperativity: VP1 units do not assemble one by one independently, but promote each other's joining. Cooperative assembly explains how hundreds of proteins form one exact shell, a puzzle shared by many viruses.
plos-pone-0000865:
Shawna MacDonald, Gang Song and Chi-Sang Poon asked how breathing syncs with a ventilator, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. Keeping a patient's breath in step with the machine is a major concern in intensive care. Lung volume feedback helps set the breathing rhythm, while steady pressure support can push against that rhythm if nothing balances it.

The authors focus on a simple form of learning, one that does not link two events together. They test whether this kind of learning helps the breathing system settle into the machine's pattern. The question matters for anyone designing ventilator care that works with the body rather than against it.
plos-pone-0000965:
Marybeth Langer, Lynn Sniderhan, Ueli Grossniklaus and colleagues described jumping genes leaving from an unusual site, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Transposable elements are DNA stretches that move around the genome and reshape it over time. Humans carry no active ones now, but our ancestors did, and their marks remain.

The team focus on excision, the cutting out step, happening at an atypical site. An odd exit point can create a new kind of element in the process. Cases like this show genomes are not fixed texts. They are edited by their own moving parts, sometimes in ways no one predicted.
plos-pone-0001065:
Hiroshi Akashi, Piyush Goel and Anoop John tested how well ancestral sequences can be inferred in fruit flies, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Reading the past state of a gene is critical to spotting the pattern and causes of molecular evolution. Among close relatives, that inference is usually assumed to be robust, but tests of the assumption were limited.

The team examine codon bias evolution in the Drosophila melanogaster subgroup. Codon bias is the uneven use of equivalent DNA spellings for the same building block. If ancestral calls are shaky, conclusions about bias may be too. Their check is methodological ground clearing for a busy field.
plos-pone-0001165:
Before a cell divides, a checkpoint makes sure every chromosome is properly attached to the spindle, the machine that pulls chromosomes apart. Théodora Niault, Khaled Hached, and Rocío Sotillo studied a checkpoint protein called Mad2 in female mouse meiosis, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Meiosis is the special division that makes eggs and sperm.

The authors changed Mad2 levels and watched chromosome segregation and checkpoint control in meiosis I. Too much Mad2 is known to hold cells in a prolonged arrest. Their work shows how sensitive egg formation is to the dose of a single checkpoint protein. That matters, because segregation errors cause miscarriage and birth defects.
plos-pone-0001265:
MicroRNAs, tiny regulators of gene activity, were still being discovered species by species in 2007. Thomas Sandmann and Stephen Cohen reported new ones for the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster in a PLOS ONE article that year. The full set of microRNAs was not known for any species, and many were believed to await discovery.

Working from the fly's recently assembled genome, the authors identified novel microRNAs and described how they found them. Each addition to the catalogue sharpens the picture of post-transcriptional regulation in development and disease. The fly, a workhorse of genetics, gains a fuller parts list.
plos-pone-0001365:
Rats communicate with ultrasonic calls that humans cannot hear. Markus Wöhr and Rainer Schwarting asked what one common call type means, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Rats emit distinct types of ultrasonic vocalizations depending on age, state, and environment. The 50-kilohertz calls have been proposed as indices of a positive subjective state, a kind of animal contentment.

The authors tested whether playback of 50-kHz calls can induce approach behavior in listening rats. If the calls signal something good, listeners should move toward the sound. Their experiment speaks to how researchers read emotion in laboratory animals, where welfare and data quality both depend on it.
plos-pone-0001465:
Mahamadou Thera and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a malaria shot tested in Mali. The shot targets a protein on the blood stage of the malaria parasite. The trial enrolled adults who face seasonal malaria in west Africa. It was a phase 1 trial, the first step, focused on safety.

Adults were split at random to get the shot or a control, with the dose raised in steps. The team tracked side effects and immune response in each group. A safe profile with a clear response would earn a trial in children. That is the group malaria hits hardest, so each step toward it counts.
plos-pone-0001565:
Mark Ungrin and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on growing human embryo stem cell clumps. Such clumps are the standard way to coax the cells to mature. But hand made clumps vary a lot in size and yield. That spread blurs tests and blocks scale up for care. The team built a way to form clumps in a uniform way.

Their method starts from single cells and yields clumps of set size at high rates. Uniform clumps give cleaner drug and growth tests. They also bring stem cell care closer to a true product. The work fixes a dull but real block in the field.
plos-pone-0001665:
Isabel Leroux-Roels, Roger Bernhard, Pascal Gérard, and their co-authors tested a bird flu vaccine in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The vaccine was built against clade 1 H5N1, one family of the bird flu virus. It was mixed with an adjuvant, an added ingredient that boosts immune responses. A vaccine stockpiled before a pandemic must also work against other families of the virus now spreading in birds.

The team checked whether the clade 1 vaccine raised cross-reactive immunity against clade 2 viruses. The full text gives the trial design, the antibody results, and how broad the protection looked. Broad cross-clade cover is a stated requirement for a pre-pandemic vaccine plan, so these results spoke directly to how health agencies should prepare.
plos-pone-0001765:
Anita M. Hennige and co-authors studied a liver protein tied to fatty liver and metabolic syndrome in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Fetuin-A is secreted by the liver and rises in hepatic steatosis and metabolic syndrome. Those states come with low-grade inflammation and low levels of adiponectin, a protective fat-tissue hormone.

The team hypothesized fetuin-A helps drive both faults, and report that fetuin-A induces cytokine expression while suppressing adiponectin production. The full text gives the cell and tissue experiments. A single liver protein that fans inflammation and cuts a protective hormone is a plausible drug target. It sits in the cluster of disorders around type 2 diabetes.
plos-pone-0001865:
Bas B. van Rijn, Arie Franx, Eric A. P. Steegers, and their co-authors tested immune receptor genes in dangerous pregnancy disorders in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Altered maternal inflammatory responses play a role in preeclampsia and the HELLP syndrome, a severe variant involving hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets. Both can kill mother and baby.

The team examined whether variants of the innate immune receptors TLR4 and NOD2, plus a pro-inflammatory phenotype, affect susceptibility to early-onset preeclampsia and HELLP. The full text gives the patient groups and the genetic results. Inherited inflammation settings could one day flag high-risk pregnancies early.
plos-pone-0001965:
Leah Owen and co-authors traced how a cancer-driving fusion protein mutes genes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, EWS/FLI, is the master driver of Ewing sarcoma, a bone cancer of the young. Gene studies in a sarcoma cell line had shown the fusion switches more genes off than on. That makes it act in large part as a repressor.

The team followed one target, a gene switch called NKX2.2. As the title states, EWS/FLI represses genes through NKX2.2 during the shift to cancer. Naming the middleman gives drug work a new point of attack in a cancer with few options.
plos-pone-0002065:
Joseph Yu and co-authors followed HIV patients who moved clinics, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Long-term retention on antiretroviral therapy in Africa's fast-growing programs was said to be sixty percent at two years. Yet many program reports said little about patients who transferred out to another facility, though Malawi's national figures showed transfers are common.

A patient counted as lost at one clinic may be in care at the next. The team asked what happens to those who transfer out. Fair counting matters: if transfers are thriving elsewhere, programs look worse than they are, and tracing efforts go to the wrong people.
plos-pone-0002165:
Albert Salehi, Sandra Meidute Abaraviciene, Javier Jimenez-Feltstrom, and co-authors studied faulty insulin release in diabetic rats, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In type 2 diabetes, the beta cells of the pancreas fail to answer rising blood sugar as they should, and in time they fail outright. The team suspected that too much nitric oxide made inside the pancreatic islets plays a part in that failure.

They used GK rats, a strain that develops type 2 diabetes on its own. In these animals, high islet nitric oxide went along with abnormal hormone release. A gut hormone, GLP-1, countered the effect, a clue for how GLP-1 based drugs may protect beta cells.
plos-pone-0002265:
Ivo Dinov, Daniel Rubin, William Lorensen, and co-authors presented a framework for organizing the tools of computational biology, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Progress in the field rests on three legs: new algorithms, systems to manage data resources, and tools that can work together. Without order, valuable resources sit scattered and hard to find.

iTools is a system for classifying, categorizing, and integrating computational biology resources in one registry. It gives researchers a single place to describe and locate tools and data. Shared registries of this kind keep a fast-growing field from drowning in its own output.
plos-pone-0002365:
Songkun Su, Fang Cai, Aung Si, and co-authors showed that Asian honeybees can read the dances of European honeybees, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The waggle dance lets foragers advertise the place of a food source to hive mates. It is famed as the only known form of symbolic communication in an invertebrate. Whether different honeybee species use the same code was an open question.

In mixed colonies, Asiatic honeybees understood the dance language of European honeybees and found the advertised food. The shared code hints that the dance dialects of bee species rest on a common, older system of spatial communication.
plos-pone-0002465:
Preisser and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Evan L. Preisser, Daniel I. Bolnick, among others. Its subject is the Many Faces of Fear: Comparing the Pathways and Impacts of Nonconsumptive Predator Effects on Prey Populations. Most ecological models assume that predator and prey populations interact solely through consumption: predators reduce prey densities by killing and consuming individual prey.

However, predators can also reduce prey densities by forcing prey to adopt costly defensive strategies. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002565:
Xu, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Dao-Zhen Xu, Kai Zhao, Li-Min Guo, among others. Its subject is a Randomized Controlled Phase IIb Trial of Antigen-Antibody Immunogenic Complex Therapeutic Vaccine in Chronic Hepatitis B Patients. The safety of the immune complexes composed of yeast-derived hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002665:
In 2008, Albert Nienhaus and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was Interferon-Gamma release assay for the diagnosis of latent TB infection – analysis of discordant results, when compared to the tuberculin skin test. The catalog record names Albert Nienhaus first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. With the Interferon-γ release assays (IGRA) a new method for the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis infections (LTBI) is available. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002765:
In 2008, Chanaz Salmi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about squalamine: an appropriate strategy against the emergence of multidrug resistant Gram-Negative bacteria?. Authorship is credited in the record to Chanaz Salmi and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. We reported that squalamine is a membrane-active molecule that targets the membrane integrity as demonstrated by the ATP release and dye entry. A further point appears in the abstract. In this context, its activity may depend on the membrane lipid composition. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002865:
Jinze Xu and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of iron accumulation with age, oxidative stress and functional decline. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Jinze Xu, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Identification of biological mediators in sarcopenia is pertinent to the development of targeted interventions to alleviate this condition. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002965:
Davendra Sohal, Andrew Yeatts, Kenny Ye and co-authors combined many microarray studies of blood stem cells in 2008. Microarrays measure gene activity across the genome, and vast data had built up across labs. Combining it is hampered by differing platforms and gene labels between studies.

Their meta-analysis found a novel signature, a shared gene pattern, for hematopoietic progenitor cells, the parents of blood cells. It also showed that data from different platforms can be integrated. Published in PLOS ONE, the paper is both a result and a proof that careful pooling of public data pays off.
plos-pone-0003065:
Qing-Bai She, Sarat Chandarlapaty, Qing Ye and co-authors studied breast tumor response to Akt signaling in a 2008 PLOS ONE article that was later retracted. Faulty PI3K/Akt signaling is common in breast cancers, arising from HER2 amplification, PI3K mutation, or PTEN loss. The objective was to test how Akt activation's role depends on which mechanism switched it on.

Readers should note the retraction status in the catalog title before citing any finding. The paper asked whether tumor cells with PI3K mutation or HER2 amplification depend selectively on Akt. Treat its claims as withdrawn unless independently confirmed elsewhere.
plos-pone-0003165: Hemant Kulkarni and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on judging AIDS risk in people infected with HIV-1. The title states its claim: a combined gene pattern, CCL3L1-CCR5 genotype, improves how well AIDS risk can be assessed. No abstract text beyond the title was supplied, so this record adds no data on methods or effect sizes.
plos-pone-0003265:
Deb K. Chatterjee, Kalavathy Sitaraman, Cassio Baptista and colleagues describe a protein array made on demand in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They describe a novel, simple and low-cost protein microarray strategy wherein arrays are generated by printing expression-ready plasmid DNAs onto slides. Those slides can be converted into protein arrays on demand, as the printed plasmids serve dual purposes.

Readers learn how storing DNA instead of protein can solve the fragility of protein chips. Proteins decay fast, while printed DNA keeps until needed. A cheaper, storable array could widen proteomics work beyond specialist centres.
plos-pone-0003365:
Mathieu Lihoreau, Cédric Zimmer and Colette Rivault test mutual mate choice in cockroaches in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Theoretical models of sexual selection predict both males and females of many species should benefit by selecting their mating partners. However, empirical evidence testing and validating this prediction is scarce. In particular, inbreeding avoidance is expected to influence choice by both sexes.

The title states when it pays both sexes to avoid inbreeding, under mutual mate choice. Readers get a rare two-sided test, since most mate choice studies examine females alone. Avoiding inbreeding is a benefit clear enough for both sexes to act on.
plos-pone-0007465: The tobacco hornworm moth and the silkworm are distant cousins, and this study compared their chromosomes with glowing DNA probes. The maps revealed long stretches of genes sitting in the same order in both species — conserved synteny — across hundreds of millions of years of separation. The work gives insect researchers a shortcut for transferring gene knowledge between species.
plos-pone-0007565: A hydrogen-making enzyme got a jump-start recipe. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Kuchenreuther's team found three small molecules wake up [FeFe] hydrogenase. The enzyme drives oxygen-free hydrogen metabolism. The wake-up mix was tested in dishes. The recipe feeds green-fuel science.
plos-pone-0007665: The brain's support cells come in flavors, and this study shows two gene-silencing proteins, REST and CoREST, are deployed differently to create them. Their distinct patterns guide glial subtype identity and the maturation of myelin-making oligodendrocytes. The finding maps a control layer of brain development.
plos-pone-0007765: Chemotherapy hits everyone differently, and genes explain part of it. This study scanned the genome for variants affecting response to gemcitabine and AraC, two common cancer drugs. The associated markers could one day match patients to the drugs most likely to work.
plos-pone-0007865: Achy joints got an immune-cell stakeout. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Thurlings's team trailed monocytes into arthritic joints with scans. Macrophages drive the joint fire. The cell stakeout was mapped. The scan feeds arthritis care.
plos-pone-0007965: Tumors' neighbors got a cheerleader rap. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Liao's team showed cancer fibroblasts cheer tumor growth through immunity. Stroma cells dominate the tumor scene. The cheerleading was mapped. The rap feeds tumor immunology.
plos-pone-0008065: Cancer stem cells and normal stem cells use the same transcription factors — but to different ends. This study compared the factors' roles in normal versus transformed human stem cells. The divergent jobs reveal how cancer hijacks the stem-cell program.
plos-pone-0008165: Viruses must cross the cell's cytoplasm to reach the nucleus — a journey with an optimal strategy. This theoretical study modeled the best transport through the crowded cell. The physics reveals the constraints every invading virus faces.
plos-pone-0008265: A tick germ's disguise kit was decoded. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Foley's team showed antigen diversity in Anaplasma phagocytophilum springs from clustered pseudogenes. The tick-borne parasite shuffles these spare parts to dodge immunity. The team mapped the selectively kept decoys. The shuffling system explains the germ's staying power.
plos-pone-0008365: Grape data got a unifying network. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Grimplet's team built VitisNet to integrate grapevine omics through molecular networks. Genome, transcript, protein, and metabolite data had piled up separately. The network weaves them into one map. The integration turns data heaps into biological insight.
plos-pone-0008465: Losing photosynthesis was found beating gaining it. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by de Castro's team examined why eukaryotes ditch photosynthesis more often than they gain it. The trait arose at least nine times yet is lost repeatedly. The team weighed the driving forces. The loss bias reshapes views of algal evolution.
plos-pone-0008565: MRI contrast got a water-physics check. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Chen and Kim characterized T1rho dispersion of water proton relaxation in protein solutions and tissue. Image contrast hinges on water's magnetic behavior. The dispersion curves reveal the hidden physics. The check sharpens clinical MRI.
plos-pone-0008665: Breast cancer's spread got a DNA-tag fingerprint. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Andrews's team refined the DNA-methylation signature of breast cancer spread using multi-platform chip scans. The tangled tag changes were decoded. The sharper signature may flag the most dangerous tumors. The fingerprint could steer care.
plos-pone-0008765: Mad-cow disease's human form got a U.S. body map. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Notari's team detected prion protein across organs in an American variant CJD case. The beef-linked prion's spread was charted. The multiorgan map informs prion science.
plos-pone-0008865: Moral math got a gender brain check. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Fumagalli's team asked whether gender shapes utilitarian decisions in the brain. The cold-calculus choices were scanned. The gender difference was measured. The check informs moral neuroscience.
plos-pone-0008965: Tick germs got a glow-tag switch. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Baldridge's team used the rickettsial ompB promoter to drive GFP in transformed Rickettsia montanensis. The gene-expression tool was validated. The switch aids tick-borne disease research.
plos-pone-0009065: Heart-risk proteins got a people split. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Kim's team split 47 heart-risk proteins by sex and roots. The clinic group's gaps were mapped protein by protein. The split feeds tailored heart care. The gaps may explain risk differences.
plos-pone-0009165: A cough syrup's kin got a swelling fight. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Zughaier's team found cough-syrup kin fight swelling hard. The plant-kin win was logged. The win hints at new swelling drugs.
plos-pone-0009265: Flower sweets got a plant-juice story. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Radhika's team found plant juice steers flower sweets. The juice-sweet link was mapped. The story feeds bee science. The sweets lure the pollinators.
plos-pone-0009365: Brain tumors versus radiation scars got a cell-spy test. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Arbab's team used magnetically labeled T-cells and MRI to tell glioma from radiation injury. The differentiation method was tested. The test feeds neuro-oncology.
plos-pone-0011465: Macrophages are immune cells that spot germs through sensors called Toll-like receptors, then sound cytokine alarms. This research paper names Themis2, also called ICB1, as a helper protein that tunes that alarm chain. The find adds a new control knob on the immune front line, with promise for calming out-of-control inflammation.
plos-pone-0011565: Carbon monoxide is famous as a silent killer, but tiny doses may calm inflammation. This research paper tests inhaled carbon monoxide for safety and efficacy during lung inflammation in mice. The paradoxical therapy — poison as medicine — probes whether the gas can soothe injured lungs without harming the animal.
plos-pone-0011665: Anthrax spores must break into cells to kill, and they hijack the cell's own machinery to do it.
